Content:
Recall that if [MATH: (\rho, \theta, \phi)] are the spherical polar coordinates of a point [MATH: P] in the three-dimensional space, then its Cartesian coordinates [MATH: (x,y,z)] can be found using the following formulas:

Content:
[MATH: x = \rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \qquad
y = \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \qquad
z = \rho\cos\phi]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/dddb0b4fb69364436d9daf3f58d65e7c]

Content:
With that in mind, let's find a parametrization of the sphere whose cartesian equation is

Content:
[MATH: x^2+y^2+z^2=1.]

Content:
This equation represents a unit sphere (i.e., a sphere of radius [MATH: 1]) centered at the origin.

Content:
Given a point [MATH: P] on the sphere, the variable [MATH: \rho] represents the radial distance between the origin and [MATH: P.] Since every point on the sphere is a distance of [MATH: 1] from [MATH: O,] we must have [MATH: \rho =1] at every point on the sphere.

Content:
Therefore, for any point [MATH: (x,y,z)] on our surface, we obtain the following:

Content:
[MATH: f(θ, ϕ)|= ⟨x, y, z⟩; = ⟨ρ\cos θ\sin ϕ, ρ\sin θ\sin ϕ, ρ\cos ϕ⟩; = ⟨1 ⋅ \cos θ\sin ϕ, 1 ⋅ \sin θ\sin ϕ, 1 ⋅ \cos ϕ⟩; = ⟨\cos θ\sin ϕ, \sin θ\sin ϕ, \cos ϕ⟩]

Content:
where [MATH: \theta \in [0,2\pi)] and [MATH: \phi \in [-\pi,\pi].]
As a result, the vector-valued function

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{f}(\theta,\phi) = \big\langle \cos\theta\sin\phi, \: \sin\theta\sin\phi, \: \cos\phi \big\rangle,
\qquad \theta \in [0,2\pi), \quad \phi \in [-\pi,\pi],]

represents a parametrization of our sphere.

[MATH: \mathbf{f}(\theta,\phi) = \big\langle 5 \cos\theta\sin\phi, \: \text{_____}, \: 5 \cos\phi \big\rangle]

The vector-valued function [MATH: \mathbf{f}(\theta,\phi)] above parametrizes the sphere defined in Cartesian coordinates as [MATH: x^2+y^2+z^2=25.] What is the second component of [MATH: \mathbf{f}?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The given equation generates a sphere of radius [MATH: 5] centered at the origin. In spherical polar coordinates, this sphere has the equation [MATH: \rho =5.]

If [MATH: (\rho, \theta, \phi)] are the spherical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates [MATH: (x,y,z)] can be found using the following formulas: [MATH: x = \rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \qquad y = \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \qquad z = \rho\cos\phi.]

Now, for any point [MATH: (x,y,z)] on our surface, we obtain the following:

[MATH: f(θ, ϕ)|= ⟨x, y, z⟩; = ⟨ρ\cos θ\sin ϕ, ρ\sin θ\sin ϕ, ρ\cos ϕ⟩; = ⟨5 ⋅ \cos θ\sin ϕ, 5 ⋅ \sin θ\sin ϕ, 5 ⋅ \cos ϕ⟩; = ⟨5\cos θ\sin ϕ, 5\sin θ\sin ϕ, 5\cos ϕ⟩]

where [MATH: \theta \in [0,2\pi)] and [MATH: \phi \in [-\pi,\pi].]

Therefore, the second component of [MATH: \mathbf{f}] is [MATH: {\color{black} 5 \sin\theta\sin\phi}.]

The vector-valued function [MATH: \mathbf{f}(\theta,\phi)] above parametrizes the ellipsoid defined in Cartesian coordinates as

[MATH: \dfrac{x^2}{36}+\dfrac{y^2}{25}+\dfrac{z^2}{16}=1.] What is the first component of [MATH: \mathbf{f}?]

The vector-valued function [MATH: \mathbf{f}(\theta,\phi)] above parametrizes the ellipsoid defined in Cartesian coordinates as

[MATH: \dfrac{x^2}{36}+\dfrac{y^2}{25}+\dfrac{z^2}{16}=1.]
What is the first component of [MATH: \mathbf{f}?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, we make the following substitution:

[MATH: x = 6X, \qquad y =5 Y, \qquad z = 4Z]

Substituting the above into the Cartesian equation of our ellipsoid, we get

[MATH: X^2 + Y^2 + Z^2 = 1,]

which is the equation of a sphere of radius [MATH: 1] centered at the origin in [MATH: (X,Y,Z)] coordinates. In spherical polar coordinates, this sphere has the equation [MATH: \rho =1.]

If [MATH: (\rho, \theta, \phi)] are the spherical polar coordinates of a point, then its [MATH: (X,Y,Z)] coordinates can be found using the following formulas: [MATH: X = \rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \qquad Y = \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \qquad Z = \rho\cos\phi.]

Now, for any point [MATH: (x,y,z)] on our surface, we obtain the following:

[MATH: f(θ, ϕ)|= ⟨x, y, z⟩; = ⟨6X, 5Y, 4Z⟩; = ⟨6ρ\cos θ\sin ϕ, 5ρ\sin θ\sin ϕ, 4ρ\cos ϕ⟩; = ⟨6 ⋅ 1 ⋅ \cos θ\sin ϕ, 5 ⋅ 1 ⋅ \sin θ\sin ϕ, 4 ⋅ 1 ⋅ \cos ϕ⟩; = ⟨6\cos θ\sin ϕ, 5\sin θ\sin ϕ, 4\cos ϕ⟩]

where [MATH: \theta \in [0,2\pi)] and [MATH: \phi \in [-\pi,\pi].]

Therefore, the first component of [MATH: \mathbf{f}] is [MATH: {\color{black}6\cos\theta\sin\phi}.]

[MATH: \mathbf{f}(r,\theta) = \big\langle \text{_____}, \: 6r\sin\theta, \: r \big\rangle, \qquad r \geq 0]

The vector-valued function [MATH: \mathbf{f}(r,\theta)] above parametrizes the half-cone defined in Cartesian coordinates as

[MATH: z^2=\dfrac{x^2}{25}+\dfrac{y^2}{36}, \qquad z\geq 0.]

What is the first component of [MATH: \mathbf{f}?]

What is the first component of [MATH: \mathbf{f}?]

sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, we make the following substitution:

[MATH: x = 5X, \qquad y = 6Y, \qquad z = Z]

Substituting the above into the Cartesian equation of our half-cone, we get

[MATH: Z^2=X^2+Y^2,\qquad Z\geq 0]

which is the equation of a half-cone whose axis of symmetry is the [MATH: Z]-axis in [MATH: (X,Y,Z)] coordinates. In cylindrical polar coordinates, this cone has the equation [MATH: Z = r.]

If [MATH: (r, \theta, Z)] are the cylindrical coordinates of a point, then its [MATH: (X,Y,Z)] coordinates can be found using the following formulas:

[MATH: X = r\cos\theta, \qquad Y = r\sin\theta, \qquad Z = Z.]

Now, for any point [MATH: (x,y,z)] on our surface, we obtain the following:

[MATH: f(r, θ)|= ⟨x, y, z⟩; = ⟨5X, 6Y, Z⟩; = ⟨5 ⋅ r\cos θ, 6 ⋅ r\sin θ, Z⟩; = ⟨5r\cos θ, 6r\sin θ, r⟩]

where [MATH: r \in [0,\infty)] and [MATH: \theta \in [0,2\pi).]

Therefore, the first component of [MATH: \mathbf{f}] is [MATH: {\color{black} 5r\cos\theta}.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Recall that if [MATH: (\rho, \theta, \phi)] are the spherical polar coordinates of a point [MATH: P] in the three-dimensional space, then its Cartesian coordinates [MATH: (x,y,z)] can be found using the following formulas:

Content:
[MATH: x = \rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \qquad
y = \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \qquad
z = \rho\cos\phi]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/dddb0b4fb69364436d9daf3f58d65e7c]

Content:
With that in mind, let's find a parametrization of the sphere whose cartesian equation is

Content:
[MATH: x^2+y^2+z^2=1.]

Content:
This equation represents a unit sphere (i.e., a sphere of radius [MATH: 1]) centered at the origin.

Content:
Given a point [MATH: P] on the sphere, the variable [MATH: \rho] represents the radial distance between the origin and [MATH: P.] Since every point on the sphere is a distance of [MATH: 1] from [MATH: O,] we must have [MATH: \rho =1] at every point on the sphere.

Content:
Therefore, for any point [MATH: (x,y,z)] on our surface, we obtain the following:

Content:
[MATH: f(θ, ϕ)|= ⟨x, y, z⟩; = ⟨ρ\cos θ\sin ϕ, ρ\sin θ\sin ϕ, ρ\cos ϕ⟩; = ⟨1 ⋅ \cos θ\sin ϕ, 1 ⋅ \sin θ\sin ϕ, 1 ⋅ \cos ϕ⟩; = ⟨\cos θ\sin ϕ, \sin θ\sin ϕ, \cos ϕ⟩]

Content:
where [MATH: \theta \in [0,2\pi)] and [MATH: \phi \in [-\pi,\pi].]
As a result, the vector-valued function

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{f}(\theta,\phi) = \big\langle \cos\theta\sin\phi, \: \sin\theta\sin\phi, \: \cos\phi \big\rangle,
\qquad \theta \in [0,2\pi), \quad \phi \in [-\pi,\pi],]

Content:
represents a parametrization of our sphere.

Content:
Watch out! There are many possible parameterizations of the given sphere. Here, we found one of them.
